answer: A festival I thoroughly enjoy celebrating is Eid, which is one of the most important occasions in my culture. There are actually two Eids each year, but the one after Ramadan is my favourite, because it follows a month of fasting and reflection. The day begins with special prayers at the Eidgah, the open prayer ground, followed by visiting relatives, exchanging gifts and, of course, an enormous feast. The atmosphere is wonderfully [[joyous]], with everyone dressed in their finest clothes and children excitedly collecting small gifts of money, which we call salami. I celebrate it with my entire extended family, which is a big part of why I love it so much. We usually spend it at my grandparents' village home, and my elder sister travels up from Dhaka with her husband and children, so the house is full of noise and laughter. My four-year-old nephew always comes straight to me for his salami. What I enjoy most is the strong sense of [[togetherness]] it creates; in our busy lives, it is one of the few times the whole family gathers. The food, prepared over several days by my mother and grandmother, is absolutely [[delectable]]. Honestly, the warmth and generosity that fill the day are genuinely heartwarming. It is far more than a religious occasion; it is a celebration of family, gratitude and community, and many people share food with neighbours and those less fortunate. I always look forward to it, and it leaves me feeling deeply [[content]] and grateful for the people in my life.

followUps.q: What is your favourite Eid dish?
followUps.answer: Definitely my mother's shemai, a sweet vermicelli dish cooked with milk and sugar. Eid morning doesn't feel complete until I have had a bowl of it, usually before we even leave for prayers.

followUps.q: Is Eid celebrated differently in cities and villages?
followUps.answer: A little. In Dhaka it can feel quieter, because so many people travel back to their home districts. In villages it is more communal, with the whole neighbourhood visiting each other's houses throughout the day.
